content.content:
1	# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)
2	
3	The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.
4	
5	Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.
6	
7	## Where this departs from the issue
8	
9	- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
10	- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
11	- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
12	- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
13	- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
14	- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
15	- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
16	- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.
17	
18	## The record
19	
20	No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie named for the server (below) and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.
21	
22	`identity.json`'s `certificate` is untouched: today's self-signed certificate (`remote.rs:101–106`, no subject alternative names) stays exactly as it is. A browser will warn about it, and clicking through is the trust step, said in the dialog. A trusted-certificate path is a follow-up with its own issue (Left for the owner).
23	
24	The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.
25	
26	## The signals
27	
28	None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.
29	
30	## The actions and effects
31	
32	**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`).**
33	
34	- **Cookie.** `/pair` takes an optional `"transport": "cookie"` in its body (additive; a native client omits it). With it, the reply carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, where `<server_id>` is the `server_id` in the same reply (`app.rs:3663`, the identity's UUID, hyphenated, so a valid cookie-name token), and the body **omits `token`**, so the page's script never holds it. Without it, the reply is unchanged. `read_request` takes `cookie`, `origin` and `host` into new `RemoteRequest` fields; the struct literal is at `remote.rs:506` only (Settled, tree bullet 1). `authenticate` (`app.rs:3127`) uses the bearer if present, else the value of the cookie named `__Host-sb-<this host's server_id>`, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header and every other cookie ignored.
35	  - **Why the name carries the id.** Cookies ignore ports, so two Switchboard instances on one Mac (two ports, one address) share one cookie jar for the page's host; a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. Each instance reads and writes only its own name. The `server_id` is stable across a key rotation (`make_identity` keeps it, `adapters/remote.rs:93–100`), so a rotation does not orphan the cookie, and the page needs no knowledge of the name: it is `HttpOnly` and the host builds it.
36	  - Where the credential lives is the security decision, so this is the safer store: a cookie the page's script cannot read, not `localStorage`, and not a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. Settled gives the mechanics for the socket (cookies ride the handshake, credentials mode `include`); whether Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host is **Unresolved 3**. It is the first thing the implementer tests (see Order of work), on today's certificate. If it fails in a browser, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner (below), not a second transport built now.
37	  - **Limits, stated.** A cookie is not scoped by port, so another HTTPS service the owner runs on the same address receives it; the per-server name keeps Switchboard instances apart, not other services. `__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port. The prefix is enforced by the browser (`Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`).
38	  - **Cross-site writes.** A request authenticated by cookie alone must, if it is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`; otherwise 403, code `origin`. A bearer request is exempt (native clients send no `Origin`). `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the cookie cross-site; this closes the same-site, other-port case.
39	- **Reply headers.** `RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:388`) gains `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>`, written by `respond` (`remote.rs:530`). There are about twenty literals in `src/app.rs` plus the one in `connection` (Settled, tree bullet 1): add `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)` and convert them mechanically, so the one site that sets a header says so. `respond` also adds `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every JSON reply, which no client reads.
40	- **`GET /api/v1/me`**, read scope, answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}` from the authenticated device and the identity. It is not in `capabilities`: no Swift client calls it.
41	
42	**Pages, answered on the connection thread.** `GET /`, `GET /app.js` and `GET /app.css`, matched exactly, are answered in `connection` (`remote.rs:770`) from a new `src/adapters/web.rs` that holds the table of path, `Content-Type` and `include_str!` body. They never reach the frame: the bytes are constant, a page load must not wait on a busy frame, and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound (`remote.rs:580`) is for work the core does. Anything else outside `/api/v1/` still reaches the frame and gets today's JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023`), `/favicon.ico` included; `index.html` declares `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so a browser has no reason to ask. A query on a page path is ignored and never logged (the connection thread logs nothing of a request).
43	
44	- Headers on every page reply: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Connection: close`. No inline script, no inline style, no external resource. If a browser does not admit `wss:` under `connect-src 'self'`, the socket is what is lost and polling carries; that is the enhancement stance, not a gap in the base.
45	- **Pool and window.** A page request is an unauthenticated connection: it counts in the 4-connection pool from accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and `Connection: close` frees the slot at once instead of holding it for the 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`). That choice does not wait on the browser's connection count (Unresolved 6); the implementer measures five parallel connections against the harness and records it in the spike. A new `Limits.page` window allows 120 page requests a minute per listener, 429 past it (a load is three; `/pair` stays at 6 and `/info` at 60, `remote.rs:583–587`). The existing pool and rate tests count `/pair` and `/info` only, so they are undisturbed; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the one extended.
46	- **What the page shows with no fragment and no token:** a "Not paired" screen that says to open the pairing window on the Mac and scan its code, with no host name. Its one request is `/me`, answered 401.
47	
48	**Certificate.** No change: no reissue, no export, no new action or effect. Whether Chrome and Safari offer a click-through for a certificate with no SAN, and whether the exception persists, is Unresolved 1; the default (the one built) is the click-through, which is what the owner chose, and the page, the polling and the acceptance steps assume only that the browser has been let through. A browser that offers no way past the warning cannot load the page at all; that case is the trusted-certificate follow-up, not machinery here.
49	
50	**Pairing invite.** A pure `invite_url(identity, window, address, port) -> String` in `src/core/remote.rs` builds the fragment URL, so the UI holds no logic and a test can call it. `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` calls it. The QR and "Copy invite" both carry the URL (decision 3 in the issue: one QR; the headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code, and the CLI and the paste field parse text, so nothing needs the JSON form on the wire). The Swift side is where the old text was parsed: `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:113–116`) accepts the URL as well as the JSON, and `main.swift:111`, `BrowserView.swift:103–107` and `:883` already go through it. A build that predates this cannot paste the new text; its Bonjour path is unchanged.
51	
52	## The UI
53	
54	The page (`web/`), one screen at a time, plain DOM with `textContent` only (no `innerHTML`, which keeps agent output from becoming markup):
55	
56	- **Boot.** Read `location.hash`; if it holds `code`, `key` and `id`, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` first, hold the values in memory, `GET /api/v1/info`, and compare `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the URL's. Mismatch: "This address is a different Switchboard than the code was for", nothing sent. Match: `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` and go to the list. Errors by `error.code`: `pairing_closed`, `wrong_code`, `wrong_key`, `rate_limited` each have a sentence.
57	- **No fragment.** `GET /api/v1/me`. 200: the list. 401: the inference from `/info` described above, or "Not paired" when nothing is stored.
58	- **Header.** Host name and the device's scope word, from `/me`.
59	- **List.** `/projects`, then `/projects/{id}/sessions` each, grouped by project, a project with a waiting session first, waiting sessions first within it. A waiting row says "Waiting on you" and `waiting_reason` in words (not colour alone), then name, kind, card word, time since `last_activity_ms`.
60	- **Session.** A Claude Code session (`kind: claude`) shows `/sessions/{id}/last-response`; any other kind shows `/sessions/{id}/screen`. The reply box shows when `/me` says `control` and `prompt_refusal` is null; with a refusal it shows the refusal's text and no box. Send is `POST /sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with `op` random hex (made from `getRandomValues`, which exists without a secure context), kept so a retry after a dropped reply repeats the same op and is answered from `operations.log` rather than typed twice. A 403 `scope` re-reads `/me`. "Sent" means accepted; the session's card moving is the progress, per §4.5.
61	- **Refresh.** Every 3 s while the tab is visible the page reads `/waiting` and compares its `epoch` and `revision` with those of the list it holds; a different one refetches the list and the open session. A reply older than the one applied is dropped (§4.4). When the socket connects (`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, no subprotocol), a `changed` frame triggers the same refetch at once and the poll slows to 20 s; on `resync_required`, a close or an error, the page refetches, polls at 3 s again, and retries the socket after 5 s doubling to 60 s. The page sends no `watch` frames: reading a content key puts it in the watch set for a minute (§4.4, item 3), and the poll keeps it warm.
62	- **Every 401** from any call runs the `/info` inference.
63	- **Device name** from the user agent: browser (`Edg`, `Chrome`, `Firefox`, else `Safari`) "on" device (`iPhone`, `iPad` including a Macintosh UA with touch, `Android`, `Mac`, `Windows`, `Linux`), else "Browser".
64	
65	The dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`):
66	
67	- The pairing section shows the QR from the URL and keeps the code, key and address lines. When the port is Mac-only it says so in place of the address. No new button.
68	- A sentence beside the existing redaction one (`remote.rs:70–76`): a browser cannot pin this Mac's key; it will warn about the certificate, and proceeding past the warning is the trust step, so proceed only if the address is this Mac's; pair a browser only on a network you trust; the code works once. The sentence promises nothing about which browsers allow the proceed.
69	- Browsers appear in the devices list like any device, with the user-agent name, scope and Revoke.
70	
71	## The tests
72	
73	- **Core (`src/core/tests.rs`).** `invite_url`: fragment form, no `?`, address and port, the loopback case.
74	- **Adapters.** None new; the certificate and the stores are unchanged.
75	- **Host (`tests/remote.rs`, a helper beside `http`/`call` at `:245–325` that sends headers and returns the response head).**
76	  - Each of the three paths answers 200 with its `Content-Type`, the CSP exactly, `no-store`, `nosniff`, `Connection: close`, to an unpaired client; `/favicon.ico`, `POST /` and `/api` still get the JSON 404; a query is not echoed.
77	  - The embedded page references only paths the host serves: `index.html`'s `src` and `href` values are in the table or `data:`; every `/api/v1/...` string in `app.js` (kept in one table with `{id}` placeholders so a test can read it) answers something other than `not_found` for a paired device. Guards: no `<script>` without `src`, no `on…=` attribute and no `style=` in `index.html`; no `innerHTML`, `eval` or `document.write` in `app.js`.
78	  - The pairing flow end to end, as the CLI does it: `/info`, then `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` gives a `Set-Cookie` named `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (the `server_id` in the reply body) with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and a body with no `token`; the cookie alone reads `/me`; a native pair is unchanged (token in the body, no cookie). Two hosts, as two instances on one Mac: each pairs and gets a differently named cookie; a request carrying both cookies is authenticated by each host as its own device, and a request carrying only the other host's cookie is 401. A cookie under the fixed name `__Host-sb` authenticates nothing.
79	  - `Origin`: a cookie `POST send` with no `Origin` or the wrong one is 403 `origin`; with `https://<host>` it runs; the same with a bearer needs none; a cookie upgrade with a foreign `Origin` is refused and with the right one is 101 (`subscribe_at`, `:1960`, takes extra headers).
80	  - `/me` shows `read`, then `control` after `SetDeviceScope`. After revoke, the cookie gets 401 `unauthorized` and `/info` returns the same `server_id` and key, which is what the page's inference needs. A rotated identity (`:1423`) returns a different key.
81	  - Pool and window: `Connection: close` frees the slot (four sequential page loads, then a fifth succeeds); four stalled strangers still make a fifth page request fail at accept; the 121st page request in a minute is 429 while `/info` and `/pair` windows are unaffected.
82	  - The sessions, waiting and last-response shapes the page reads are already pinned by the shared fixtures; no fixture changes, since no Swift speaker reads `/me`.
83	- **UI (`tests/ui.rs`, rewrite the assertions at `~:7476–7493`).** "Copy invite" puts the URL on the clipboard with the window's code and the identity's key in its fragment; the Mac-only notice shows when `listen.lan` is off.
84	- **Swift (`client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:157–165`).** The URL parses to the same `PairingInvite`; the JSON still does; a URL without `code` is an error. The URL's shape is repeated inline, as the JSON's is.
85	- **The page's logic.** `app.js` keeps its pure parts (fragment parse, device name, the `/info` inference, revision ordering) behind a guarded `module.exports`, and `web/app.test.js` covers them with `node --test`. A Rust test runs it and skips cleanly when `node` is absent, like the tmux tests. Nothing drives a real browser: the spike and the owner's phone do.
86	
87	## Order of work
88	
89	One commit; the app runs at each step.
90	
91	1. **Spike `spikes/23-web-page/`** (the next free number at the time; 22 is `remote-port`): a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as `make_identity` makes it today (P-256, no SAN), a page whose server sets `__Host-sb-<id>` (`HttpOnly`) and reads it back by `fetch`, in Chrome and Safari on the Mac with the certificate exception accepted, with a second server on another port setting its own id's cookie to see that neither overwrites the other; plus the CSP `wss:` question and five parallel connections against the harness. README with the commands and what was seen. If no browser can be driven, the README says "not run" and acceptance steps 1 to 4 rest on the owner's phone.
92	2. `RemoteReply::new` and headers, `RemoteRequest` fields, `respond`.
93	3. Cookie in `authenticate`, `Origin` rule, `/pair` transport, `/me`.
94	4. `web.rs`, page paths in `connection`, `Limits.page`.
95	5. `invite_url`, the dialog, the Swift parse.
96	6. `web/`.
97	7. Docs: `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1 (page requests in the unauthenticated pool and `Limits.page`), §4.3 (the `/me` row and the page paths, auth "none"), line 207 (the excerpt), §5 lines 306, 312 and 319 (pre-pairing surface; fragment invite; cookie named for the server id, `Origin` rule, "never in a URL" still true; the browser's weaker trust), a dated line in §0; `docs/design.md` a dated paragraph at the end of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (before `## Versioning and updates`, `:3585`) and its known gaps; `README.md` Layout rows for `web/`, `src/adapters/web.rs` and the spike, and the dev-aid sentence at `:276–278` (the invite is now a URL; `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"` takes it); `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased: "The remote port serves a web page: pair a phone's browser from the pairing window's QR, see the waiting sessions, read the last response or screen and send a reply."
98	
99	## Left for the owner
100	
101	- **If the cookie test fails in a browser:** the fallback is the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo (Unresolved 3). It puts the token where script can read it, so it is the owner's call, and a plan of its own.
102	- **A trusted-certificate path, its own issue.** This plan leaves today's certificate as it is and makes the click-through the trust step. If the owner's phone offers no way past the warning (Unresolved 1), or the exception does not persist, or iOS needs a trusted certificate for `wss://` (Unresolved 2), the way out is a certificate a device can trust: IP subject alternative names (which Chrome needs, Settled "Certificate trust"), a way to get the file onto the device, or a local CA that signs the certificate. Each touches the identity model or the trust boundary, so it is a design decision for the owner and a separate issue.
103	- **The one-line excerpt** on the wire: move the card's excerpt out of `src/ui/cards.rs` into the core and add an additive `SessionView` field.
104	- **Owner's phone, branches that do not change this plan:** does the camera scan open the page and does the warning let you proceed (yes: the dialog's sentence is true as written; no: the trusted-certificate issue above is the path); does `changed` arrive without a reload on iOS Safari (the poll already moves the list); does the phone reach the Mac (the dialog states the listen requirement); does the phone show "removed on the host" after Revoke (the inference needs only the two assertions above).
105	
106	## Contract additions (copy into the commit)

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

The host serves a small page from the port it already has. A phone opens it from the pairing window's QR, pairs, lists the sessions with the waiting ones first, reads a session's last response or screen, and sends a reply. The page is three embedded files (`web/index.html`, `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`) with no build step and no dependency. It speaks the protocol the headset speaks.

Yardstick for the world outside this tree: `facts.md` for #230. Where a decision rests on a line under Settled, the line is cited. Where it rests on a line under Unresolved or For the owner, the decision says so, and the default is the design that works whichever way the answer goes. Line numbers are from this worktree at `7fe8949`.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **The code travels in the URL fragment, not the query.** The issue's `/?code=…&key=…&id=…` puts the code in the request line of the first `GET`, so a server the owner has not verified receives it before any script runs, and `read_request` hands the query to the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:495–503`). A fragment is not part of the request target and is never sent (Settled, "Fragment and query"; RFC 9110 §4.2.5). The URL is `https://<address>:<port>/#code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`. The page still calls `history.replaceState` before anything else; whether Safari keeps the full URL in an earlier history entry is Unresolved 4, so the code's single use does the rest: `Paired` closes the window (`src/core/remote.rs:65`), and a leaked URL is inert after the first pairing.
- **The key in the URL is not authentication in a browser.** The issue says the comparison lets a genuine page refuse to send the code to a host whose `/info` key differs. A browser cannot see which certificate it is talking to, so a relay that terminates TLS and forwards to the real host shows the page the real key and the comparison passes. The plan keeps the comparison (it catches a QR for another host, and a stale one) and says in the dialog that it is not a defence. A browser pairing is weaker than a native one, which pins the key out of band; the dialog says "pair a browser only on a network you trust".
- **The one-line excerpt is not on the wire, and the spec says it is.** `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card's excerpt is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook "on the record". `src/core/events.rs:127–135` stores only `last_stop_at` and `pending_at_stop`; `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–689`) has no excerpt; the Mac computes it in the UI from the transcript (`src/ui/cards.rs:176–185`, `558–575`). Storing it would change `SessionRecord` (`src/core/model.rs:1053`, `SCHEMA_VERSION` 16) and moving the function would be a change of its own. This cut: a row shows the name, kind, the card word, `waiting_reason`, and the time since `last_activity_ms`; the excerpt is a follow-up. The same commit corrects line 207 to say the excerpt is not on the port yet.
- **"Revoked" cannot be said by the host.** Revoke deletes the `PairedDevice` (`src/core/remote.rs:86–92`), so a revoked token and an unknown one are the same 401 `unauthorized` (`src/app.rs:3142–3149`; Settled, tree bullet on 401). The page infers it from `/info`, which it can read unauthenticated: a 401 with the stored `server_id` and `spki_sha256` unchanged says "this device was removed on the host; pair again"; a different key or id says "identity changed, pair again"; no answer says "can't reach the host". No host change, and no new error code that could not be told the truth.
- **The events socket is an enhancement, not the base.** The issue has the page open `/api/v1/events` directly and meets "moves to the top without a reload" with it. Safari does not support `wss://` to a self-signed certificate even when trusted (Settled, "Certificate trust"), and a failed handshake exposes only close code 1006 (Settled, "WebSocket in browsers"). The base is polling the same REST routes, applying replies by revision as §4.4 says; the socket, when it connects, makes a change arrive at once. Acceptance steps 2 and 3 are met by polling on every browser.
- **The device cannot read its own scope back, so the issue's "hidden when the device lacks `control`" needs one small route.** `scope` in `/info` is the listing parameter, not a device property, and the tree has no `/me` (`src/app.rs:3027–3031`, `3044–3116`). The plan adds `GET /api/v1/me`.
- **The QR names an address the port may not answer on.** `src/ui/remote.rs:157–164` takes `local_address()` whatever `listen.lan` says. The URL uses it only when the port listens on the network, and `127.0.0.1` otherwise, with a line in the window saying the port is Mac-only.
- **Pre-pairing surface.** `docs/remote-client.md:306` and `:319` (and §4.3, line 194) give `/info` and `/pair`. It becomes those two and the three page paths; the plan amends them.

## The record

No record changes. `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16, `src/core/model.rs:12`), `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (7, `model.rs:612`) and `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (1, `src/ports/remote.rs:17`) do not move. `devices.json` gains no field: a browser is a `PairedDevice` whose `name` is the body's `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650–3655`, capped at 64 in `src/core/remote.rs:169`), which the page sets from its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); its scope is the pairing window's. The page keeps nothing the host needs; the browser keeps the token in an `HttpOnly` cookie named for the server (below) and, in `localStorage`, only `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}`, which is public and is what lets a later 401 be told from a changed key.

`identity.json`'s `certificate` is untouched: today's self-signed certificate (`remote.rs:101–106`, no subject alternative names) stays exactly as it is. A browser will warn about it, and clicking through is the trust step, said in the dialog. A trusted-certificate path is a follow-up with its own issue (Left for the owner).

The pairing window stays in memory and unsaved (`src/core/remote.rs:46–54`). The page's rehydration after a restart is a request: `/me` with the cookie.

## The signals

None new. The waiting mark is `SessionView.waiting` and `waiting_reason`; "moves to the top" is the revision in every envelope changing (`src/app.rs:3730–3741`) or a `changed` frame (§4.4). The host emits nothing the headset does not already receive.

## The actions and effects

**Host transport (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/app.rs`).**

- **Cookie.** `/pair` takes an optional `"transport": "cookie"` in its body (additive; a native client omits it). With it, the reply carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>; Max-Age=34560000; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, where `<server_id>` is the `server_id` in the same reply (`app.rs:3663`, the identity's UUID, hyphenated, so a valid cookie-name token), and the body **omits `token`**, so the page's script never holds it. Without it, the reply is unchanged. `read_request` takes `cookie`, `origin` and `host` into new `RemoteRequest` fields; the struct literal is at `remote.rs:506` only (Settled, tree bullet 1). `authenticate` (`app.rs:3127`) uses the bearer if present, else the value of the cookie named `__Host-sb-<this host's server_id>`, matched by exact name in the `Cookie` header and every other cookie ignored.
  - **Why the name carries the id.** Cookies ignore ports, so two Switchboard instances on one Mac (two ports, one address) share one cookie jar for the page's host; a fixed name would have the second pairing overwrite the first's token. Each instance reads and writes only its own name. The `server_id` is stable across a key rotation (`make_identity` keeps it, `adapters/remote.rs:93–100`), so a rotation does not orphan the cookie, and the page needs no knowledge of the name: it is `HttpOnly` and the host builds it.
  - Where the credential lives is the security decision, so this is the safer store: a cookie the page's script cannot read, not `localStorage`, and not a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value. Settled gives the mechanics for the socket (cookies ride the handshake, credentials mode `include`); whether Safari and Chrome store and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set from a user-accepted certificate on an IP-literal host is **Unresolved 3**. It is the first thing the implementer tests (see Order of work), on today's certificate. If it fails in a browser, the fallback is a follow-up for the owner (below), not a second transport built now.
  - **Limits, stated.** A cookie is not scoped by port, so another HTTPS service the owner runs on the same address receives it; the per-server name keeps Switchboard instances apart, not other services. `__Host-` fixes the host and path, not the port. The prefix is enforced by the browser (`Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`).
  - **Cross-site writes.** A request authenticated by cookie alone must, if it is not a `GET`, or is an upgrade, carry `Origin: https://<Host header>`; otherwise 403, code `origin`. A bearer request is exempt (native clients send no `Origin`). `SameSite=Strict` already withholds the cookie cross-site; this closes the same-site, other-port case.
- **Reply headers.** `RemoteReply` (`remote.rs:388`) gains `headers: Vec<(&'static str, String)>`, written by `respond` (`remote.rs:530`). There are about twenty literals in `src/app.rs` plus the one in `connection` (Settled, tree bullet 1): add `RemoteReply::new(status, body, authenticated)` and convert them mechanically, so the one site that sets a header says so. `respond` also adds `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` to every JSON reply, which no client reads.
- **`GET /api/v1/me`**, read scope, answers `{device_id, name, scope, server_id, server_name}` from the authenticated device and the identity. It is not in `capabilities`: no Swift client calls it.

**Pages, answered on the connection thread.** `GET /`, `GET /app.js` and `GET /app.css`, matched exactly, are answered in `connection` (`remote.rs:770`) from a new `src/adapters/web.rs` that holds the table of path, `Content-Type` and `include_str!` body. They never reach the frame: the bytes are constant, a page load must not wait on a busy frame, and the `DRAIN_PER_PASS` bound (`remote.rs:580`) is for work the core does. Anything else outside `/api/v1/` still reaches the frame and gets today's JSON 404 (`app.rs:3023`), `/favicon.ico` included; `index.html` declares `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so a browser has no reason to ask. A query on a page path is ignored and never logged (the connection thread logs nothing of a request).

- Headers on every page reply: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, and `Connection: close`. No inline script, no inline style, no external resource. If a browser does not admit `wss:` under `connect-src 'self'`, the socket is what is lost and polling carries; that is the enhancement stance, not a gap in the base.
- **Pool and window.** A page request is an unauthenticated connection: it counts in the 4-connection pool from accept (`remote.rs:701–706`), and `Connection: close` frees the slot at once instead of holding it for the 30 s idle timeout (`remote.rs:573`). That choice does not wait on the browser's connection count (Unresolved 6); the implementer measures five parallel connections against the harness and records it in the spike. A new `Limits.page` window allows 120 page requests a minute per listener, 429 past it (a load is three; `/pair` stays at 6 and `/info` at 60, `remote.rs:583–587`). The existing pool and rate tests count `/pair` and `/info` only, so they are undisturbed; `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool…` (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the one extended.
- **What the page shows with no fragment and no token:** a "Not paired" screen that says to open the pairing window on the Mac and scan its code, with no host name. Its one request is `/me`, answered 401.

**Certificate.** No change: no reissue, no export, no new action or effect. Whether Chrome and Safari offer a click-through for a certificate with no SAN, and whether the exception persists, is Unresolved 1; the default (the one built) is the click-through, which is what the owner chose, and the page, the polling and the acceptance steps assume only that the browser has been let through. A browser that offers no way past the warning cannot load the page at all; that case is the trusted-certificate follow-up, not machinery here.

**Pairing invite.** A pure `invite_url(identity, window, address, port) -> String` in `src/core/remote.rs` builds the fragment URL, so the UI holds no logic and a test can call it. `src/ui/remote.rs:160–166` calls it. The QR and "Copy invite" both carry the URL (decision 3 in the issue: one QR; the headset pairs from Bonjour and a typed code, and the CLI and the paste field parse text, so nothing needs the JSON form on the wire). The Swift side is where the old text was parsed: `PairingInvite.parse` (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:113–116`) accepts the URL as well as the JSON, and `main.swift:111`, `BrowserView.swift:103–107` and `:883` already go through it. A build that predates this cannot paste the new text; its Bonjour path is unchanged.

## The UI

The page (`web/`), one screen at a time, plain DOM with `textContent` only (no `innerHTML`, which keeps agent output from becoming markup):

- **Boot.** Read `location.hash`; if it holds `code`, `key` and `id`, call `history.replaceState(null, '', location.pathname)` first, hold the values in memory, `GET /api/v1/info`, and compare `spki_sha256` and `server_id` with the URL's. Mismatch: "This address is a different Switchboard than the code was for", nothing sent. Match: `POST /api/v1/pair {code, spki_sha256, device_name, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store `{server_id, spki_sha256, server_name}` and go to the list. Errors by `error.code`: `pairing_closed`, `wrong_code`, `wrong_key`, `rate_limited` each have a sentence.
- **No fragment.** `GET /api/v1/me`. 200: the list. 401: the inference from `/info` described above, or "Not paired" when nothing is stored.
- **Header.** Host name and the device's scope word, from `/me`.
- **List.** `/projects`, then `/projects/{id}/sessions` each, grouped by project, a project with a waiting session first, waiting sessions first within it. A waiting row says "Waiting on you" and `waiting_reason` in words (not colour alone), then name, kind, card word, time since `last_activity_ms`.
- **Session.** A Claude Code session (`kind: claude`) shows `/sessions/{id}/last-response`; any other kind shows `/sessions/{id}/screen`. The reply box shows when `/me` says `control` and `prompt_refusal` is null; with a refusal it shows the refusal's text and no box. Send is `POST /sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` with `op` random hex (made from `getRandomValues`, which exists without a secure context), kept so a retry after a dropped reply repeats the same op and is answered from `operations.log` rather than typed twice. A 403 `scope` re-reads `/me`. "Sent" means accepted; the session's card moving is the progress, per §4.5.
- **Refresh.** Every 3 s while the tab is visible the page reads `/waiting` and compares its `epoch` and `revision` with those of the list it holds; a different one refetches the list and the open session. A reply older than the one applied is dropped (§4.4). When the socket connects (`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, no subprotocol), a `changed` frame triggers the same refetch at once and the poll slows to 20 s; on `resync_required`, a close or an error, the page refetches, polls at 3 s again, and retries the socket after 5 s doubling to 60 s. The page sends no `watch` frames: reading a content key puts it in the watch set for a minute (§4.4, item 3), and the poll keeps it warm.
- **Every 401** from any call runs the `/info` inference.
- **Device name** from the user agent: browser (`Edg`, `Chrome`, `Firefox`, else `Safari`) "on" device (`iPhone`, `iPad` including a Macintosh UA with touch, `Android`, `Mac`, `Windows`, `Linux`), else "Browser".

The dialog (`src/ui/remote.rs`):

- The pairing section shows the QR from the URL and keeps the code, key and address lines. When the port is Mac-only it says so in place of the address. No new button.
- A sentence beside the existing redaction one (`remote.rs:70–76`): a browser cannot pin this Mac's key; it will warn about the certificate, and proceeding past the warning is the trust step, so proceed only if the address is this Mac's; pair a browser only on a network you trust; the code works once. The sentence promises nothing about which browsers allow the proceed.
- Browsers appear in the devices list like any device, with the user-agent name, scope and Revoke.

## The tests

- **Core (`src/core/tests.rs`).** `invite_url`: fragment form, no `?`, address and port, the loopback case.
- **Adapters.** None new; the certificate and the stores are unchanged.
- **Host (`tests/remote.rs`, a helper beside `http`/`call` at `:245–325` that sends headers and returns the response head).**
  - Each of the three paths answers 200 with its `Content-Type`, the CSP exactly, `no-store`, `nosniff`, `Connection: close`, to an unpaired client; `/favicon.ico`, `POST /` and `/api` still get the JSON 404; a query is not echoed.
  - The embedded page references only paths the host serves: `index.html`'s `src` and `href` values are in the table or `data:`; every `/api/v1/...` string in `app.js` (kept in one table with `{id}` placeholders so a test can read it) answers something other than `not_found` for a paired device. Guards: no `<script>` without `src`, no `on…=` attribute and no `style=` in `index.html`; no `innerHTML`, `eval` or `document.write` in `app.js`.
  - The pairing flow end to end, as the CLI does it: `/info`, then `/pair` with `transport: "cookie"` gives a `Set-Cookie` named `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (the `server_id` in the reply body) with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, and a body with no `token`; the cookie alone reads `/me`; a native pair is unchanged (token in the body, no cookie). Two hosts, as two instances on one Mac: each pairs and gets a differently named cookie; a request carrying both cookies is authenticated by each host as its own device, and a request carrying only the other host's cookie is 401. A cookie under the fixed name `__Host-sb` authenticates nothing.
  - `Origin`: a cookie `POST send` with no `Origin` or the wrong one is 403 `origin`; with `https://<host>` it runs; the same with a bearer needs none; a cookie upgrade with a foreign `Origin` is refused and with the right one is 101 (`subscribe_at`, `:1960`, takes extra headers).
  - `/me` shows `read`, then `control` after `SetDeviceScope`. After revoke, the cookie gets 401 `unauthorized` and `/info` returns the same `server_id` and key, which is what the page's inference needs. A rotated identity (`:1423`) returns a different key.
  - Pool and window: `Connection: close` frees the slot (four sequential page loads, then a fifth succeeds); four stalled strangers still make a fifth page request fail at accept; the 121st page request in a minute is 429 while `/info` and `/pair` windows are unaffected.
  - The sessions, waiting and last-response shapes the page reads are already pinned by the shared fixtures; no fixture changes, since no Swift speaker reads `/me`.
- **UI (`tests/ui.rs`, rewrite the assertions at `~:7476–7493`).** "Copy invite" puts the URL on the clipboard with the window's code and the identity's key in its fragment; the Mac-only notice shows when `listen.lan` is off.
- **Swift (`client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:157–165`).** The URL parses to the same `PairingInvite`; the JSON still does; a URL without `code` is an error. The URL's shape is repeated inline, as the JSON's is.
- **The page's logic.** `app.js` keeps its pure parts (fragment parse, device name, the `/info` inference, revision ordering) behind a guarded `module.exports`, and `web/app.test.js` covers them with `node --test`. A Rust test runs it and skips cleanly when `node` is absent, like the tmux tests. Nothing drives a real browser: the spike and the owner's phone do.

## Order of work

One commit; the app runs at each step.

1. **Spike `spikes/23-web-page/`** (the next free number at the time; 22 is `remote-port`): a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as `make_identity` makes it today (P-256, no SAN), a page whose server sets `__Host-sb-<id>` (`HttpOnly`) and reads it back by `fetch`, in Chrome and Safari on the Mac with the certificate exception accepted, with a second server on another port setting its own id's cookie to see that neither overwrites the other; plus the CSP `wss:` question and five parallel connections against the harness. README with the commands and what was seen. If no browser can be driven, the README says "not run" and acceptance steps 1 to 4 rest on the owner's phone.
2. `RemoteReply::new` and headers, `RemoteRequest` fields, `respond`.
3. Cookie in `authenticate`, `Origin` rule, `/pair` transport, `/me`.
4. `web.rs`, page paths in `connection`, `Limits.page`.
5. `invite_url`, the dialog, the Swift parse.
6. `web/`.
7. Docs: `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1 (page requests in the unauthenticated pool and `Limits.page`), §4.3 (the `/me` row and the page paths, auth "none"), line 207 (the excerpt), §5 lines 306, 312 and 319 (pre-pairing surface; fragment invite; cookie named for the server id, `Origin` rule, "never in a URL" still true; the browser's weaker trust), a dated line in §0; `docs/design.md` a dated paragraph at the end of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (before `## Versioning and updates`, `:3585`) and its known gaps; `README.md` Layout rows for `web/`, `src/adapters/web.rs` and the spike, and the dev-aid sentence at `:276–278` (the invite is now a URL; `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"` takes it); `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased: "The remote port serves a web page: pair a phone's browser from the pairing window's QR, see the waiting sessions, read the last response or screen and send a reply."

## Left for the owner

- **If the cookie test fails in a browser:** the fallback is the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo (Unresolved 3). It puts the token where script can read it, so it is the owner's call, and a plan of its own.
- **A trusted-certificate path, its own issue.** This plan leaves today's certificate as it is and makes the click-through the trust step. If the owner's phone offers no way past the warning (Unresolved 1), or the exception does not persist, or iOS needs a trusted certificate for `wss://` (Unresolved 2), the way out is a certificate a device can trust: IP subject alternative names (which Chrome needs, Settled "Certificate trust"), a way to get the file onto the device, or a local CA that signs the certificate. Each touches the identity model or the trust boundary, so it is a design decision for the owner and a separate issue.
- **The one-line excerpt** on the wire: move the card's excerpt out of `src/ui/cards.rs` into the core and add an additive `SessionView` field.
- **Owner's phone, branches that do not change this plan:** does the camera scan open the page and does the warning let you proceed (yes: the dialog's sentence is true as written; no: the trusted-certificate issue above is the path); does `changed` arrive without a reload on iOS Safari (the poll already moves the list); does the phone reach the Mac (the dialog states the listen requirement); does the phone show "removed on the host" after Revoke (the inference needs only the two assertions above).

## Contract additions (copy into the commit)

- No new `AppAction` or `Effect` variant, no port method.
- `RemoteReply.headers`, `RemoteReply::new`; `RemoteRequest.{cookie, origin, host}`.
- `core::remote::invite_url`.
- Wire: `GET /api/v1/me`; `/pair` request field `transport`; the `__Host-sb-<server_id>` cookie accepted as a credential beside the bearer header; the 403 code `origin`; `GET /`, `/app.js`, `/app.css` before pairing; the invite text is a URL (the JSON still parses in the Swift client).
- No change to `model.rs`, `control/`, or any schema version.

# Spike 23: a browser on the remote port

The questions the web control surface (#230) rests on that no source
settled (`facts.md` for #230, Unresolved 3 and 6): does a browser store
and send a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie set by a
self-signed certificate with no subject alternative name on an
IP-literal host once the owner has clicked through its warning; do two
servers on one address with per-server cookie names (`__Host-sb-<id>`)
keep their cookies apart; does the page's `connect-src 'self'` admit
`wss:` to the same host; and how many of a browser's parallel
connections a page load costs against the port's pool of four.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

## What it does

`src/main.rs` is a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as
the app's `make_identity` makes it (P-256, self-signed, CN only). It
serves one page under the app's exact Content-Security-Policy whose
script asks `/set` to set `__Host-sb-<id>=tok-<id>` as an `HttpOnly`
cookie, reads `/me` back (the server echoes the `Cookie` header it
received), prints `document.cookie` (which should be empty), and opens
`wss://<host>/ws`, reporting `open`, `error` or the close code. Two
servers with different `--id` and `--port` on one address show whether
the second's cookie overwrites the first's: after both pages have
loaded, `/me` on either should list both cookies, each under its own
name.

## Commands

```sh
cd spikes/23-web-page
cargo run --release -- --port 8443 --id alpha      # one terminal
cargo run --release -- --port 8444 --id beta       # another
# On the Mac: open https://127.0.0.1:8443/ and https://127.0.0.1:8444/ in
# Safari and in Chrome, proceed past the certificate warning, read the
# <pre>. On a phone: the Mac's LAN address in place of 127.0.0.1.
```

Headless Chrome with `--ignore-certificate-errors` is a weaker check
(it bypasses the warning rather than recording an exception) and is
how the Mac half can be driven without a hand:

```sh
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8443/
chrome --headless=new --ignore-certificate-errors --user-data-dir=/tmp/sb-spike23 \
  --virtual-time-budget=6000 --dump-dom https://127.0.0.1:8444/
```

## Results (2026-10-24)

**Browser: not run.** The implementing session could run the servers
but not a browser, so the cookie, the two-server jar and the `wss:`
questions stand as the plan left them: acceptance steps 1 to 4 rest on
the owner's phone and on the two commands above. The host side builds
to the favourable answer (the cookie transport) and the fallback the
plan names (the token held by the page with a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`
echo) is the owner's call if a browser refuses the cookie.

**Parallel connections against the harness: measured.** The test
`page_loads_free_their_slot_and_have_their_own_window` in
`tests/remote.rs` opens five page requests at once against the real
listener's unauthenticated pool of four, each reply closing its
connection:

| run | served |
|---|---|
| five parallel `GET /app.js` | 4 of 5 |

The fifth is dropped at accept because the four are still inside their
TLS handshakes when it arrives; a browser retries a dropped connection,
and a page load is three requests, so a single phone never meets the
limit. Five sequential loads all succeed, which is what `Connection:
close` buys: a kept connection would hold a slot for the 30 s idle
timeout. The test asserts at least four and prints the count with
`--nocapture`.

servers on one address with per-server cookie names (`__Host-sb-<id>`)
keep their cookies apart; does the page's `connect-src 'self'` admit
`wss:` to the same host; and how many of a browser's parallel
connections a page load costs against the port's pool of four.

Standalone crate, not built by the app. Builds into the repo's shared
`target/` like every crate under this tree.

`src/main.rs` is a throwaway HTTPS server over a certificate made as
the app's `make_identity` makes it (P-256, self-signed, CN only). It
serves one page under the app's exact Content-Security-Policy whose
script asks `/set` to set `__Host-sb-<id>=tok-<id>` as an `HttpOnly`
cookie, reads `/me` back (the server echoes the `Cookie` header it
received), prints `document.cookie` (which should be empty), and opens
`wss://<host>/ws`, reporting `open`, `error` or the close code. Two
servers with different `--id` and `--port` on one address show whether
the second's cookie overwrites the first's: after both pages have
loaded, `/me` on either should list both cookies, each under its own
name.

```sh
cd spikes/23-web-page
cargo run --release -- --port 8443 --id alpha      # one terminal
cargo run --release -- --port 8444 --id beta       # another

# Safari and in Chrome, proceed past the certificate warning, read the
# <pre>. On a phone: the Mac's LAN address in place of 127.0.0.1.
```

how the Mac half can be driven without a hand:

# Correctness review, head fd5295b (round 1)

I read the host side (`src/adapters/remote.rs`, `web.rs`, `app.rs` authenticate/pair/me, `core/remote.rs`), `web/app.js`, the UI dialog change and the test list against the plan. No record type changes, so no `SCHEMA_VERSION` step is owed. I did not run the test suite or a browser. The host side matches the plan: cookie by exact per-server name, bearer preferred, the `Origin` rule applied to non-GET and upgrades, the body omits `token` under `transport: cookie`, and pages are answered on the connection thread with `Connection: close`. Points below, most severe first.

## 1. A reply being typed is wiped by any refresh (`web/app.js` `renderSession`, `loadSession`, `poll`)

State: a `control` device has a session open and is typing in the textarea, and the agent is working. Every host revision change (any session activity, not only this one) makes `poll` see a different `/waiting` revision. It calls `refetchAll`, which calls `loadSession`, which calls `renderSession`. `renderSession` runs `clear()` and builds a new textarea. The draft is restored only from `state.pending`, and that is set only inside `sendReply`. So the typed text disappears, with focus, caret and the phone keyboard state, every few seconds while the agent is active. Waiting on the agent and then replying is the main use of the page, and this makes typing a reply unreliable exactly then. The socket path (`changed` leads to `refetchAll`) does the same.

Failing input: open a claude session whose agent is mid-turn, type "yes, go ahead" slowly, and the box empties on the next revision tick.

Needed: keep the compose box across a refetch. Either update only the `<pre>` text and the mark when the same session is already rendered, or save `box.value` into state before `clear()` and restore it after. Neither the plan's Refresh section nor `app.test.js` covers this, because the logic is in the untested browser half.

## 2. The Mac-only notice is wrong in one reachable state (`src/ui/remote.rs`, `pairing`)

`on_lan = identity.listen.lan && address.is_some()`. With `listen.lan` on but `local_address()` returning `None`, the dialog shows `MAC_ONLY_NOTICE`, "allow devices on the local network…". That setting is already on, so the owner is told to enable something that is enabled. `invite_url` does put loopback in the QR in that state, so the URL is right and only the sentence is wrong. This is a small fix: split the two causes, or word the notice as "no network address found". No UI test covers the `lan` on, no address case (it needs `local_address` injected). The plan's test only covers `lan` off.

## 3. Spike README claims a browser retry that nothing shows (`spikes/23-web-page/README.md`, results)

The README says the fifth parallel connection is "dropped at accept… a browser retries a dropped connection, and a page load is three requests, so a single phone never meets the limit". The measurement is 4 of 5 served. Nothing shows a browser retries a connection that is closed with no bytes, and browsers open up to 6 parallel connections to one host. The README itself says the browser half was "not run". The test only asserts `served >= 4`. This is an unverified claim written as a result. If the retry does not happen, a page load on a phone could lose `/app.js` or `/app.css` and show a blank or unstyled page, with nothing on the page to say why. Please soften the claim to "not measured against a browser", and have the owner's phone steps list "page loads fully on first try" among the checks.

## 4. Minor

- `authenticate` returns the `origin` refusal with `authenticated = true`. A cookie-authenticated cross-origin POST therefore moves its connection into the paired pool (`connection`, `reply.authenticated && !paired`) on the strength of a refused request. The plan does not say whether it should. It is harmless, but a refused write should not buy a paired-pool slot, so pass `false` unless the other 403s also pass `true`.
- `Limits::limited` counts any method on a page path, so `POST /` or `POST /app.js` spends the page window and then gets 429, not the JSON 404 the plan promises for them. A test of "`POST /` still gets the JSON 404" passes only because it is not run 120 times in a minute.
